218.title: An-Nazi'at: fear of standing
218.hook: whoever feared standing before his Lord and held the self from desire, the garden is home (79:40–41)
218.howItsDone: Muslims describe this as struggle with the self (jihad an-nafs): fasting, lowering the gaze, and holding the tongue in anger are all practiced as small, daily ways of restraining the self from whim.

segments.voice: Yesterday, still in An-Nazi'at: Musa sent to Pharaoh, told to open with a question. Your line was would you purify yourself.

It's eleven at night. The phone is in your hand, and the thumb already knows the way. One more video. A second slice. The reply you'd regret by morning, typed and waiting for the send button. That tiny gap between wanting something and doing it is so small that most days it goes unnoticed. Three days into An-Nazi'at, the surah ends its argument inside exactly that gap. After the great upheaval and the story of Musa and Pharaoh, it sorts people into two, and the second group is known by what they did in that small moment.
screen: `ELEVEN AT NIGHT, PHONE IN HAND.` → `THE GAP BETWEEN WANTING AND DOING.` → `WHERE THE SURAH ENDS ITS ARGUMENT.`

segments.voice: First the other group: whoever rebelled and chose the life of this world, the fire is home. Then the turn, in Pickthall's words: But as for him who feared to stand before his Lord and restrained his soul from lust, Lo! the Garden will be his home. Two things. The first is a fear, and a specific one: maqam rabbihi, the standing before his Lord. Commentators read it two ways. Some say it means the Day when every person will stand before Allah to give an account. Others say it means Allah standing over a person now, seeing what they do in the dark. Either way, it's the awareness of being seen, like a light switched on in a room. The second thing is the holding: the soul, the nafs, held back from al-hawa. Pickthall says lust, but hawa is wider: the pull of whim, the wind that blows the self wherever it likes. Notice what's not said. The verse doesn't condemn wanting. It names the self steered only by the wind. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ put it in a picture Bukhari records: the strong one isn't the wrestler who throws people down; the strong one controls himself when angry. And one small word at the end: home. Not reward, not prize. The Garden is where this person lives. That closes An-Nazi'at; tomorrow, one surah back, to An-Naba'.

segments.voice: Pick one small desire you already know will come today, the snack at four, the extra hour of scrolling, the sharp reply, and picture the half second before you act. Stay in that gap and breathe slowly, letting it widen a little; nothing is being taken from you, you're only noticing that you can choose. If you pray, bring to mind the standing before your Lord as you breathe.
An-Nazi'at. Those who pull out, the surah that ends by sorting people by what they did with the gap: the ones who held the self back from whim. Today's word.
Your line: hold the self back. The wanting can stay; the wind doesn't have to steer. Until tomorrow.

219.title: An-Naba': the great news
219.hook: what are they asking about, the great news (78:1–2)
219.howItsDone: Surah an-Naba' opens the thirtieth part of the Qur'an; it is often learned by heart early and recited in the prayers, and the whole juz' is named after its first word, 'amma.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of An-Nazi'at: the one who feared the standing before his Lord. Your line was hold the self back.

A town where everyone is talking about the same thing, at the market, at the well, in the evenings. Some laugh. Some are angry. Some are quietly unsettled and won't admit it. Commentators set this surah in Mecca, in a scene like that. A man in their own town was saying that after death every person would be raised to stand and give an account, and people argued about it the way a whole city argues about one piece of news. The surah steps into the noise and asks a question of its own. It's the first surah of the juz' this path has been reading backward, and its first word gives the whole juz' its name.
screen: `A WHOLE TOWN ARGUING.` → `ONE PIECE OF NEWS.` → `THE FIRST SURAH OF THE JUZ'.`

segments.voice: It begins: 'amma yatasa'alun. About what are they asking one another? 'Amma is two little words run together, 'an ma, about what, and it names the whole thirtieth part of the Qur'an: Juz' 'Amma. Then the surah answers itself: about the great news, an-naba' al-'azim, the one they disagree about. Pickthall calls it the awful tidings, awful in the old sense, full of awe. Arabic has an everyday word for news, khabar. Naba' is heavier. Al-Raghib al-Isfahani, a classical scholar of Qur'anic words, describes naba' as news of great weight, news that brings real knowledge and changes something. You don't use naba' for the weather. So what is the great news? Ibn Kathir and others say the Resurrection, the raising of the dead and the Day of account, which the surah's first hearers disputed. Some early commentators said the Qur'an itself, or the preaching of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. All three hang together: a book, brought by a messenger, announcing a Day. Then a line comes twice, and the repetition is the point: no, they will come to know; then no, they will come to know. The surah doesn't mock the question. It takes it seriously, and instead of arguing, it turns toward the world and starts pointing. For today, notice: the Qur'an's last part opens not with a command, but with a question people were already asking.
screen: `'AMMA — ABOUT WHAT?` · `NABA' — NEWS OF GREAT WEIGHT.` · `THE RESURRECTION, THE BOOK, THE MESSENGER.` · `THEY WILL COME TO KNOW.` · then, large: `THE GREAT NEWS.`

segments.voice: Let the noise of the day settle, then ask yourself the surah's question: about what am I asking? Underneath the small questions, what to eat, what to say, what to reply, there may be a bigger one, maybe about death, or meaning, or whether you're loved, or what comes after. Don't answer it; just find it, name it quietly in a few words, and let it sit, the way the surah lets its question sit.
An-Naba'. The news, news of great weight: the name of Surah 78, the first surah of the thirtieth part, which opens with the question about what. Today's word.
Your line: the great news. Not the weather: news that changes something. Day two hundred nineteen.

220.title: An-Naba': sleep as rest
220.hook: We made the earth a bed, mountains as pegs, sleep for rest, the night a cover (78:6–10)
220.howItsDone: Muslims who follow the Prophet's bedtime practice make wudu, lie on the right side, and say bismika Allahumma amutu wa ahya (in Your name, O Allah, I die and I live), with a phrase of praise for being given life again on waking.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the opening of An-Naba': about what are they asking? Your line was the great news.

Last night, at some point, you lay down, the thoughts slowed, and then, without deciding to, you were gone. Hours passed that you can't account for. Then you were back, the same person in the same bed, as if someone had pressed pause and then play. It happens every night, and it rarely gets a second thought. An-Naba' has named the great news, a Day when the dead are raised. Now it answers the doubters, and the answer surprises people. It doesn't argue at all. It points: at the ground under you, the mountains, your own pillow.
screen: `PAUSE, THEN PLAY.` → `EVERY NIGHT OF YOUR LIFE.` → `THE SURAH STOPS ARGUING AND POINTS.`

segments.voice: The surah asks a run of questions, and each one is a picture. Have We not made the earth a resting place, mihad, a word also used for a cradle or a spread bed? And the mountains as pegs, awtad, like the pegs that hold a tent down in the wind? And created you in pairs. Then the line for today: wa ja'alna nawmakum subata. And We made your sleep subat. The classical dictionaries tie subat to a root meaning to cut off, to stop, to rest; the same letters give sabt, the Sabbath. Sleep as the cutting off: the day's work and worry stop. Then the night as a garment, libas, the same word for clothing, wrapping you like a cover. And the day for earning a living. The argument is quiet but clear. You worry that raising the dead is impossible? You go through a small version every night. A verse in Surah az-Zumar says Allah takes the souls at the time of death, and takes those that have not died during their sleep, then keeps some and sends the others back until an appointed time. Muslim practice marks this at the edges of each night. At bedtime, Bukhari records, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ would say: in Your name, O Allah, I die and I live. And on waking: praise to Allah who gave us life after He had made us die, and to Him is the rising. Every morning, a rehearsal of the great news.
screen: `THE EARTH A BED, MOUNTAINS AS PEGS.` · `SUBAT — SLEEP AS THE CUTTING OFF.` · `THE NIGHT AS A GARMENT.` · `EVERY NIGHT, A SMALL RAISING.` · then, large: `SLEEP IS A SIGN.`

segments.voice: Sit or lie down, whichever your body wants, and let your eyes close. Starting at your feet, let each part go heavy, as if the earth really were a bed: legs, back, shoulders, jaw, each one done working for now, which is subat, the cutting off, in miniature. If you pray, you can say quietly, in Your name, O Allah, I die and I live, and then just rest.
An-Naba'. The great news, and the surah that answers it by pointing at the world: the earth a bed, the night a garment, and sleep made for rest. Today's word.
Your line: sleep is a sign. Your pillow is part of the argument. Sleep well tonight.

221.title: An-Naba': the Day of sorting
221.hook: the Day the trumpet sounds and you come in crowds (78:17–18)
221.howItsDone: Belief in the Last Day is one of the pillars of faith in Islam; Muslims recite surahs like an-Naba' in prayer and speak of the Day with both hope and fear, often reflecting on their deeds before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the middle of An-Naba': the earth a bed, the night a garment. Your line was sleep is a sign.

A drawer you've been stuffing for years. Receipts, cables, a birthday card, a key to nothing. Everything's in there together, and you can't tell the treasure from the junk anymore. Then one Saturday you pour it all onto the table and sort it: what matters in one pile, what doesn't in another. Things you'd forgotten turn up. A life can feel like that drawer: kindnesses and cruelties, the good day and the bad one, all mixed. An-Naba' has asked its question and pointed at the signs. Now it names the Day itself, and the name it chooses is a sorting word.
screen: `A DRAWER STUFFED FOR YEARS.` → `POURED OUT AND SORTED.` → `THE SURAH NAMES THE DAY.`

segments.voice: The verse says: inna yawm al-fasli kana miqata. The Day of fasl is an appointed time. Fasl comes from a root meaning to separate, to divide, to tell one thing from another. Pickthall translates it as Decision; others say Sorting or Judgment. In everyday Arabic the same root gives the word for a chapter of a book and for a season of the year: a section cut off from the rest. So it's the day when what was mixed is separated, and each thing is seen for what it was. Then the picture: the trumpet is blown and you come in crowds, afwaja, wave after wave of people. The surah describes the garden too, for the ones who were mindful, with gardens and cups and no idle talk. Then the Spirit and the angels stand in ranks, and no one speaks except whom the Most Merciful permits, and they say what is right. And it ends with one of the Qur'an's most human lines: on that Day a person will look at what their own hands sent ahead. Every act has already gone on before them, waiting. And the one who denied it all will say, if only I were dust. Muslims hold the Day with both hope and fear. The surah isn't naming it to scare anyone into a corner. In its picture, nothing a person did is lost in the drawer; even the smallest kindness gets found.
screen: `FASL — TO SEPARATE, TO SORT.` · `A CHAPTER, A SEASON, A DAY.` · `CROWDS, AND ANGELS IN RANKS.` · `WHAT YOUR HANDS SENT AHEAD.` · then, large: `THE DAY OF SORTING.`

segments.voice: Think of your days as a long line behind you, and without judging them, let a few rise up: one you're proud of, one you'd rather forget, one ordinary afternoon you'd almost lost. All of them are yours, and all of them went on ahead. Then turn to today, still being written, and ask what you'd like your hands to send ahead from it; one small thing is enough.
An-Naba'. The great news, and the surah that ends by naming the Day of sorting, when each person sees what their hands sent ahead. Today's word.
Your line: the day of sorting. Every act goes on ahead. That's day two hundred twenty-one.

222.title: Juz' 'Amma, the shape
222.hook: thirty-seven surahs: the Day, the orphan, the soul, the One
222.howItsDone: Muslim children often learn Juz' 'Amma first, starting from its end (An-Nas) and working backward, and its short surahs are commonly recited in the daily prayers; the thirty-part division lets a reader finish the whole Qur'an across a month, as some do in Ramadan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of An-Naba': the Day of fasl, when what was mixed is separated. Your line was the day of sorting.

Near the top of a hike, there's a moment when you turn around. The path you climbed is laid out below you, and for the first time you can see its shape: where it switched back, where it got steep, where you stopped for water. Since day one hundred fifty-nine, this path has walked backward through the last part of the Qur'an, from An-Nas on its final page to An-Naba' at the front. Yesterday it reached the start. So today, no new surah. Just a turn around, to look at the whole thing: thirty-seven surahs, and four things they keep coming back to.
screen: `TURNING AROUND NEAR THE TOP.` → `FROM AN-NAS BACK TO AN-NABA'.` → `THE WHOLE PATH IN VIEW.`

segments.voice: Juz' means a part. The Qur'an's surahs are of very different lengths, so later Muslims divided the text into thirty parts of roughly equal length, to be read in a month, a part a day, as some do in Ramadan. The division is a reading aid, not part of the revelation itself. The thirtieth part runs from Surah seventy-eight to the end, thirty-seven surahs, named for its first word, 'amma, about what. They're short, they rhyme, and several open with oaths: by the dawn, by the sun, by the fig and the olive. Under all that sound, four themes keep returning. The Day: An-Naba', Az-Zalzalah, Al-Qari'ah, the sorting and the weighing. The orphan: again and again the surahs ask who fed the orphan and who pushed him away, from Ad-Duha to Al-Ma'un. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ came from an orphan's childhood himself, which gives those verses a sound all their own. The soul: Ash-Shams swears by the soul and the One who shaped it, and says whoever purifies it has succeeded. And the One: Al-Ikhlas, four short lines on the oneness of Allah. It's often the first part children learn by heart: short enough to hold, one surah at a time, and full of those four things.

segments.voice: Let the last few weeks come back one surah at a time: the whisperer that withdraws, daybreak, Say, He is Allah, the One, the morning light of Ad-Duha, the man who frowned, the trumpet and the crowds. Don't try to remember them all; notice which ones come back on their own. Hold three of their names, and ask what each one gave you.

223.title: Reciting in prayer
223.hook: a short surah after the Fatiha in the first two units
223.howItsDone: In each unit of the prayer Muslims recite al-Fatiha, and in the first two units they add a short surah or some verses, often from Juz' 'Amma; the imam recites aloud at dawn, sunset and night, and silently at noon and afternoon.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Juz' 'Amma seen whole: the Day, the orphan, the soul, the One. Your line was the whole juz'.

The back of a mosque at sunset. The imam's voice rises: first the Fatiha, the seven verses said in every prayer. Then a pause, and something else. Tonight it's a surah about daybreak. Tomorrow it might be the one about the elephant, or the orphan, or the soul. Around the room, some who couldn't order lunch in Arabic follow every word, because they learned these short surahs as children. That's where Juz' 'Amma lives. Not on a shelf, but in the mouths of people praying, all over the world.
screen: `SUNSET, AT THE BACK OF A MOSQUE.` → `THE FATIHA, THEN SOMETHING ELSE.` → `WHERE JUZ' 'AMMA LIVES.`

segments.voice: Each prayer is made of units, rak'ahs: standing, bowing, prostrating, sitting. In every unit, standing, the one praying recites the Fatiha. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said, in a hadith Bukhari records, that there is no prayer for the one who doesn't recite the opening of the Book. In the first two units, something is added: a short surah, or a few verses from anywhere in the Qur'an. In the third and fourth, the Fatiha alone. The schools of law weigh the addition differently: the Hanafi school counts it as required, and the others count it as a strongly recommended practice of the Prophet. At dawn, sunset and night, the imam recites aloud in the first two units; at noon and afternoon, silently. So people need a store of short surahs, and Juz' 'Amma is the store. Two stories show the spirit of it. A companion named Mu'adh led his people in prayer with such a long surah that a tired man left. The Prophet corrected him and named shorter ones instead, like By the sun and By the night. Another man, leading prayer, added Say, He is Allah, the One, every single time. People mentioned it to the Prophet. Asked why, the man said it describes the Most Merciful, and he loved to recite it. The Prophet said: tell him that Allah loves him. In that report, a short surah said with love is answered with love.

224.title: Ayat al-Kursi
224.hook: the verse of the Throne: Allah, the Living, the Sustainer, neither drowsiness nor sleep (2:255)
224.howItsDone: Muslims recite Ayat al-Kursi before sleep, after the obligatory prayers, and when leaving home, seeking protection; it is widely learned by heart and often hangs in calligraphy in homes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rak'ah: the Fatiha in every unit, a short surah in the first two. Your line was a new one tonight.

Abu Hurayrah, a companion of the Prophet, was put in charge of the charity food; Bukhari tells the story. One night a man crept in and took handfuls. Abu Hurayrah grabbed him, heard he was needy, with a family to feed, and let him go. The next night, the same man, the same story. On the third night Abu Hurayrah held on, and the thief offered a trade: let me go and I'll teach you words that will protect you. When you lie down to sleep, recite the verse of the Throne. Abu Hurayrah told the Prophet, who answered: he told you the truth, though he's a liar. Today, from beyond Juz' 'Amma, a verse Muslims carry to bed: Ayat al-Kursi.
screen: `A GUARD, A THIEF, THREE NIGHTS.` → `A TRADE: WORDS FOR SLEEP.` → `HE TOLD YOU THE TRUTH.`

segments.voice: It's verse two hundred fifty-five of Surah al-Baqarah, the second surah. Pickthall: Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal. Neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him. Al-Hayy, the Living, depending on nothing. Al-Qayyum, which Pickthall calls the Eternal: the one who stands by Himself and holds everything else up. Four days ago An-Naba' called sleep a sign: we are made to stop, cut off, and come back. This verse says the one who holds everything up never does. Not even sinah, the first heaviness of the eyelids before sleep, touches Him. To Him belongs everything in the heavens and the earth. No one intercedes with Him except by His permission. He knows what is before people and what is behind them, and they grasp nothing of His knowledge except what He wills. Then the word that names the verse: kursi. In everyday Arabic, a chair. Pickthall says throne; some commentators say footstool, and one early explanation said it stands for His knowledge. It extends over the heavens and the earth, and guarding them doesn't tire Him. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ asked a companion which verse in the Book of Allah is greatest. The answer he approved: this one. The week in one picture: you held the self back, heard the great news, slept and woke, remembered the sorting, and through all of it, the verse says, the One who holds everything up does not sleep.
screen: `AL-HAYY, AL-QAYYUM.` · `NEITHER DROWSINESS NOR SLEEP.` · `KURSI — CHAIR, FOOTSTOOL, THRONE.` · `THE GREATEST VERSE.` · then, large: `HE DOES NOT SLEEP.`

segments.voice: Think of what you'll put down tonight when you sleep: the unanswered emails, the person you're worried about, the thing that isn't fixed. Set each one down, one per breath; you're allowed to stop, and the verse says the one who holds it all doesn't. If you pray, you can recite Ayat al-Kursi tonight as you lie down, as the night watch story suggests.
Ayat al-Kursi. The verse of the Throne, al-Baqarah two fifty-five: the Living, the Sustainer, whom neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes. Today's word.
Your line: he does not sleep. So you can. That's day two hundred twenty-four.
